questions.q: Telecom in a railway is best described as:
options: Its nervous system — radio, telephones and data links connecting trains, stations and Operations Control Centre (OCC)
questions.explain: Radio, phones and data links carry every command and report — if communication dies, the railway slows to its safest fallback.

questions.q: Train-to-Operations Control Centre (OCC) voice communication on Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) is based mainly on:
questions.explain: Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) radio is Long Term Evolution (LTE)-based (the 4G family), carrying European Train Control System (ETCS) data and voice; metros traditionally used Terrestrial Trunked Radio (TETRA).

questions.q: Metro systems traditionally used which radio technology?
questions.explain: Terrestrial Trunked Radio (TETRA) was the traditional metro train radio; Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) uses Long Term Evolution (LTE).

questions.q: Which services does the telecom system carry besides voice?
options: Data networks carrying signalling and Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA), plus Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) and Public Address System (PAS)/Passenger Information System (PIS) control
questions.explain: Telecom carries signalling/Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA) data, Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV), Public Address (PA)/Passenger Information System (PIS) control and the clock system, not just voice.

questions.q: The railway clock system exists to:
options: Keep synchronised time across the whole railway — critical for logs and investigations
questions.explain: One time everywhere means logs, recordings and event sequences can be matched during investigations.

questions.q: Why are operational radio/telephone channels recorded?
options: So instructions and events can be verified later, especially in investigations
questions.explain: Recorded channels only — operational instructions belong on channels that leave a record.

questions.q: Every train on the radio network has:
options: A unique radio identity linked to its train number
questions.explain: A unique identity tied to the train number means Operations Control Centre (OCC) always knows who is speaking.

questions.q: Telephone/intercom systems in operations connect mainly:
options: Operations Control Centre (OCC) with stations and key operational points
questions.explain: Intercom/telephone links are the fixed voice backbone between Operations Control Centre (OCC), stations and operational points.

questions.q: Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) in operations depends on telecom because:
options: CCTV is part of Automatic Fare Collection (AFC)
CCTV pictures travel over the telecom/data network to stations and Operations Control Centre (OCC)
questions.explain: Cameras are only useful if their pictures reach the people who act — that carriage is telecom's job.

questions.q: If the train radio fails completely, the railway's general response is to:
options: Slow to its safest fallback working as per procedure, using alternative communication means
Let drivers use personal phones as the primary system
questions.explain: Communication failure = degraded, safest-fallback working; the system never just carries on blind.

questions.q: A driver cannot contact Operations Control Centre (OCC) on the train radio. The best action is to:
options: Keep driving at full speed and hope
Ask a passenger to call OCC
Use the prescribed alternative means (e.g. other radio mode/telephone at the next station or as per procedure) and follow failure rules
questions.explain: Procedures define backup communication paths — use them and obey the failure rules for movement.

questions.q: Why must operational instructions be given only on recorded channels?
options: An unrecorded instruction cannot be proved or reconstructed later
It is a legal formality with no purpose
questions.explain: In any incident inquiry, what was said must be verifiable — hence recorded channels only.

questions.q: Public Address System (PAS)/Passenger Information System (PIS) control through telecom allows Operations Control Centre (OCC)/stations to:
options: Send announcements and display information across stations and trains in a coordinated way
questions.explain: Central Public Address (PA)/Passenger Information System (PIS) control is how one accurate message reaches every platform during a disruption.

questions.q: Data networks for signalling and Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA) must be:
options: Reliable and protected, because they carry safety and power-control information
questions.explain: Signalling and Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA) data ride on telecom — their reliability is an operational safety matter.

questions.q: The main difference between Long Term Evolution (LTE) on Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) and Terrestrial Trunked Radio (TETRA) in older metros is:
options: TETRA carries European Train Control System (ETCS) on RRTS
LTE is used only for tickets
RRTS LTE carries ETCS signalling data and voice together; TETRA was mainly a voice radio tradition in metros
questions.explain: On Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) the same Long Term Evolution (LTE) family carries both the European Train Control System (ETCS) data and operational voice.

questions.q: A station reports its intercom to Operations Control Centre (OCC) is dead but train radio is working. Operations should:
options: Use the working alternative channel, log/report the fault and get it repaired
Close the station in all cases
Ignore it — one channel is enough forever
questions.explain: Degraded communication is managed by alternatives plus fault reporting, not by panic or neglect.

questions.q: Synchronised clocks matter most when:
options: Reconstructing an incident from logs and recordings of different systems
questions.explain: If every system's clock differs, no one can prove the true sequence of events.

questions.q: Which of these belongs to the telecom family of systems?
options: The clock system (synchronised time across the railway)
questions.explain: Radio, telephones, Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) carriage, Public Address (PA)/Passenger Information System (PIS) control and the clock system are telecom; the rest belong elsewhere.

questions.q: During a major disruption, telecom's most valuable contribution is:
options: Keeping Operations Control Centre (OCC), stations, trains and field staff in one coordinated information loop
questions.explain: Coordination lives or dies on communication — telecom keeps everyone on the same picture.

questions.q: A radio message is unclear and partly missed by the driver. Correct practice is to:
options: Ask for it to be repeated/reconfirmed rather than acting on a guess
questions.explain: Safety-critical messages are never guessed — repeat and confirm (read-back discipline).

questions.q: Why does each train's radio identity matter during an emergency?
options: Operations Control Centre (OCC) can address and track instructions to the exact train involved
To display on Passenger Information System (PIS)
questions.explain: In an emergency, instructions must reach the right train unambiguously — identity makes that possible.

questions.q: If the Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) network fails at a station, the direct operational loss is:
options: Visual monitoring of platforms/areas — staff must compensate with physical presence and reporting
questions.explain: Losing Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) means losing eyes, not power — compensate with people until it is restored.

questions.q: Telecom failure affecting signalling data in European Train Control System (ETCS) territory would be serious because:
options: Movement Authority reaches trains by radio/data — without it, trains cannot be authorised normally
questions.explain: In European Train Control System (ETCS) L2 the radio IS the authority path; data failure strikes at train movement itself.

questions.q: Which statement about operational communication systems is correct?
options: They include voice radio, telephones, data networks, Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) carriage, Public Address (PA)/Passenger Information System (PIS) control and synchronised clocks
questions.explain: Telecom is a bundle of operational systems, all serving control and safety.

questions.q: A controller gives a long instruction mixing several actions. The telecom discipline expected is:
options: Speaking to several trains at once without identities
Clear, structured communication on the recorded channel, with confirmation
questions.explain: Structure, identity and confirmation are what make radio communication safe.

questions.q: The phrase 'communication dies, the railway slows to its safest fallback' teaches that:
options: Loss of communication is itself a degraded mode requiring reduced, safest working
Trains can run normally without communication
questions.explain: No communication = no normal operation; the fallback is deliberately slower and safer.

questions.q: Help points/intercoms at stations let passengers:
options: Reach staff/control for assistance or emergency information
questions.explain: Passenger help points are part of the communication family linking public to control.

questions.q: Why should personal mobile phones not replace the operational radio as the primary channel?
options: Operational channels are recorded, identity-linked and controlled; personal phones are none of these
Operations Control Centre (OCC) has no phone number
questions.explain: Record, identity and control are exactly what an official channel guarantees and a personal phone does not.

questions.q: A fault in the clock system is noticed (station clock differs from Operations Control Centre (OCC) time). It should be:
options: Reported and corrected, because unsynchronised time corrupts logs and investigations
questions.explain: Wrong time is an evidence problem — report it like any other operational fault.

questions.q: The telecom interface with signalling on Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) can be summarised as:
options: Long Term Evolution (LTE) radio carries European Train Control System (ETCS) movement authorities and voice, making telecom part of the train-control chain itself
questions.explain: On Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS), telecom is not beside the signalling system — it is inside it.

questions.q: Train radio systems provide a 'group call' facility. Its main operational use is:
options: Letting passengers talk to each other
Letting the Operations Control Centre (OCC) speak to all trains (or all stations) in an area at once, for example to announce a disruption or an instruction that affects everyone
questions.explain: In a disruption the same message must reach every train together. A group call from the Operations Control Centre (OCC) does in seconds what separate calls to each train cannot.

questions.q: On the operational radio network, an emergency call is treated differently from a routine call because it:
options: Is charged at a higher rate
Gets priority — it can override or pre-empt routine traffic so the emergency message gets through immediately
Is allowed only once a day
Must wait for the routine call to finish
questions.explain: Priority working means an emergency call never queues behind routine chatter. Getting the message through at once is itself a safety function of the telecom system.

questions.q: Continuous radio coverage inside tunnels is normally provided by:
options: A radiating ('leaky feeder') cable run along the tunnel that carries the radio signal to and from trains
Signal lamps repeated every few metres
questions.explain: Radio waves do not travel well through a tunnel on their own. A leaky feeder cable radiates the signal along the tunnel, so train radio and data links keep working underground.

questions.q: After a serious incident, the voice recordings of operational channels must be:
options: Preserved and made available for the incident investigation, so what was said and when can be established exactly
Given to the press before the inquiry
questions.explain: Recordings are evidence. Preserved voice logs let investigators rebuild the sequence of instructions and reports — one reason all operational communication stays on recorded channels.

questions.q: The direct 'hotline' telephone between the Operations Control Centre (OCC) and a station is preferred for urgent operational talk because:
options: It is cheaper than other phones
It connects instantly to the right desk without dialling or going through a switchboard, and it is a recorded operational channel
It cannot be heard by anyone else in the room
It works without any power supply
questions.explain: A hotline removes delay and wrong numbers at the worst moment: lift, speak, and the station's operational desk answers — with the conversation recorded like all safety communication.
